rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treasures of mercy signify God's gifts to all beings, with خزائن used as a metaphor for blessings.
rows.anchor: خزائن نعمه التي أفاضها على كافة الموجودات فالرحمة مجاز عن النعم والخزائن استعارة تحقيقية أو تخييلية

rows.speaker: الحوفي والزمخشري وأبو البقاء وابن عطية
rows.claim: They parse أنتم as the subject of an elided verb explained by تملكون, since لو does not normally take a noun directly.
rows.anchor: على مذهب إليه الحوفي والزمخشري وأبو البقاء وابن عطية وغيرهم فاعل لفعل محذوف يفسره المذكور

rows.speaker: حاتم والملتمس
rows.claim: Their poetic examples attest the construction with a subject before لو and an understood verb.
rows.anchor: قول حاتم وقد أسر فلطمته جارية لو ذات سوار لطمتني وقول الملتمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ellipsis is concise; repeated predication or repeated condition intensifies the warning, and the semantically fronted subject restricts the meaning to exclusive ownership, which implies shared ownership a fortiori.
rows.anchor: وفائدة الحذف والتفسير على ما قيل الإيجاز فإنه بعد قصد التوكيد لو قيل تملكون تملكون

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن علي بن فضالة المجاشعي
rows.claim: He supplies لو كنتم أنتم تملكون, treating أنتم as emphasis on the omitted pronoun; the author says this is unsound.
rows.anchor: إن التقدير لو كنتم أنتم تملكون وظاهره

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن بن الصائغ وأبو حيان
rows.claim: Ibn al-Saigh reads an omitted كان with أنتم as its noun; Abu Hayyan calls this the best parsing because deleting كان after لو is familiar Arabic usage, though the author favors his first analysis as more expressive.
rows.anchor: إن الأصل لو كنتم تملكون فحذفت كان وحدها وانفصل الضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here withholding is a metonym for the most extreme, ugly miserliness; calling a miser ممسك reflects this interpretation.
rows.anchor: فلما حذف المفعول ووجه إلى نفس الفعل بمعنى لفعلتم الإمساك جعل كناية عن أبلغ أنواعه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة والراغب
rows.claim: خشية الإنفاق means fear of poverty; al-Raghib explains أنفق as becoming poor.
rows.anchor: أي مخافة الفقر كما أخرجه ابن جرير وابن المنذر عن ابن عباس وروى نحوه عن قتادة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: He takes الإنفاق in its familiar sense of spending, with an omitted phrase meaning fear of spending's consequence.
rows.anchor: أنفق وأملق وأعدم وأصرم بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposed reading makes الإنفاق a metaphor for depletion; خشية is parsed as a causal object, while its circumstantial-masdar parse is judged unlikely.
rows.anchor: مجازا عن لازمه وهو النفاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse portrays unsurpassable stinginess: even sole control of God's inexhaustible stores would lead people to hoard from fear of poverty.
rows.anchor: وقد بلغت هذه الآية من الوصف بالشح الغاية القصوى التي لا يبلغها الوهم

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poem imagines an extreme miser refusing even a needle to Joseph, sharpening the verse's comparison with ordinary human stinginess.
rows.anchor: ولو أن دارك أنبتت لك أرضها إبرا يضيق بهل فناء المنزل وأتاك يوسف يستعيرك إبرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says his first grammatical analysis is more informative than Abu Hayyan's proposal.
rows.anchor: الكلام على ما سمعت أولا أفيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قتور means intensely miserly; قتر is reducing expenditure, the opposite of extravagance, and both extremes are blameworthy.
rows.anchor: مبالغا في البخل وجاء القتر بمعنى تقليل النفقة وهو بأزاء الإسراف وكلاهما مذموم

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: He derives the words for miserly poverty from قتار/قتر, the smoke rising from roasting food or incense.
rows.anchor: وأصل ذلك كما قال الراغب من القتار والقتر وهو الدخان الساطع من الشواء

rows.speaker: العسكري وغيره
rows.claim: They say the warning targets Meccans who demanded a spring and rivers: even with divine stores they would hoard and would not benefit anyone, so granting their requests would be pointless.
rows.anchor: وقيل الخطاب لأهل مكة الذين اقترحوا ما اقترحوا من الينبوع والأنهار

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: He links the verse to Muhammad's exceptional generosity and tireless effort to guide his kin, contrasted with their refusal to respond and their harm to him.
rows.anchor: إنه عليه الصلاة والسلام قد منحه الله تعالى ما لم يمنحه لأحد من النبوة والرسالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects Abu Hayyan's proposed connection between this verse and the preceding verses as contrary to sound taste.
rows.anchor: ولعمري إن هذا مما يأباه الذوق السليم والذهن المستقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He proposes that the verse's condemnation of excessive miserliness parallels the preceding condemnation of unbelief, whose harm extends beyond the miser's more limited harm.
rows.anchor: اشتمالها على ذمهم بالشح المفرط كما أن ما قبلها مشتمل على ذمهم بالكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After recounting Quraysh's obstinacy, the passage consoles the Prophet by recalling Moses' conflict with Pharaoh and God's punishment of Pharaoh and his people.
rows.anchor: سلاه تعالى جده بما جرى لموسى عليه السلام مع فرعون وما صنع سبحانه بفرعون وقومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context and parallels indicate nine clear proofs of Moses' prophethood; specifying nine does not deny that he received more.
rows.anchor: ظاهر السياق والنظائر يقتضيان كون المعنى تسع أدلة واضحات الدلالة على نبوة موسى

rows.speaker: بعض التفاسير
rows.claim: One enumeration follows the Torah: staff, blood, frogs, lice, livestock deaths, destructive hail with fire, locusts, darkness, and the death of firstborn humans and animals.
rows.anchor: هي كما في التوراة العصا ثم الدم ثم الضفادع ثم القمل ثم موت البهائم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report counts the staff, hand, flood, locusts, lice, frogs, blood, years of famine, and reduced produce; Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Qatada, and Ikrima also transmit this list.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما أنها العصا واليد والطوفان والجراد والقمل والضفادع والدم والسنين ونقص من الثمرات

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He treats years of famine and reduced produce as one sign; the author rejects this because the verse distinguishes them, plausibly as drought in wilderness and loss in cultivated fields.
rows.anchor: كما روي عن الحسن ورد بأنه ليس بالحسن إذ ظاهر قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report lists Moses' hand, tongue, staff, sea, flood, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood.
rows.anchor: عن الحبر أنها يده عليه السلام ولسانه وعصاه والبحر والطوفان والجراد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس في الكشاف
rows.claim: The Kashshaf list substitutes the stone and the raised Mount Sinai for years and produce; al-Kashf objects that those were not signs directed to Pharaoh, though it answers that the nine might include a subset and the sea split came at the final drowning, not as a challenge.
rows.anchor: في الكشاف عنه رضي الله تعالى عنه أنها العصا واليد والجراد والقمل والضفادع والدم والحجر والبحر والطور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He finds the first Ibn Abbas enumeration plausible, but the Kashshaf attribution to al-Hasan conflicts with the reliable books he consulted.
rows.anchor: وما روي عن ابن عباس أولا لائح الوجه ما فيه أشكال ونسبه في الكشاف إلى الحسن

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز ومحمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Asked by Umar to enumerate the signs, Muhammad ibn Ka'b included the plague; Umar praised his learning and showed a bag of split eggs, nuts, beans, chickpeas, and lentils turned to stone.
rows.anchor: أن عمر بن عبد العزيزعليه الرحمة سأل محمد بن كعب عن هذه الآيات فعد ما وعد وذكر فيه الطمس

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In a report from Safwan ibn Assal, the Prophet answers two Jewish questioners with nine universal prohibitions: idolatry, adultery, unlawful killing, theft, sorcery, usury, informing a ruler against an innocent, slandering chaste women, and fleeing battle; he adds the Sabbath restriction specially for Jews, and they affirm his prophethood.
rows.anchor: عن صفوان بن عسال أن يهوديين قال : أحدهما لصاحبه انطلق بنا إلى هذا النبي

rows.speaker: الترمذي والحاكم
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhi grades the Safwan report hasan sahih, while al-Hakim calls it sound with no known defect.
rows.anchor: والترمذي وقال حسن صحيح والحاكم وقال صحيح لا نعرف له علة

rows.speaker: الشهاب الخفاجي
rows.claim: He calls the interpretation of the nine signs as commandments the correct one, since they mark salvation for those obeying and ruin for those who do not; another explanation treats them as divine scriptural utterances signifying those laws.
rows.anchor: إنه التفسير الصحيح ووجه إطلاقها عليها بأنها علامات على السعادة

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: He says the Sabbath rule is a wise supplementary answer: after nine laws shared by all religions, the Prophet adds a Jewish-specific one, demonstrating knowledge of their law; al-Khafaji's unqualified rejection of calling this أسلوب حكيم is misplaced.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشف أنه من الأسلوب الحكيم لأنه عليه الصلاة والسلام لما ذكر التسع العامة في كل شريعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He does not accept that the signs must all concern Pharaoh; if such a link is required, some laws could have addressed Pharaoh and Israelites together.
rows.anchor: لا نسلم أنه يجب في الآيات المذكورة في الآية أن تكون مما له تعلق بفرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports supporting the miracle and commandment interpretations conflict, but the strongest support for the commandments is the wording فسل بني إسرائيل.
rows.anchor: فمؤيدات كل من التفسيرين أعني تفسير الآيات بالأدلة والمعجزات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read فسل as an imperative, apparently addressing Muhammad and asking in the usual sense; most take it as addressing Moses, with asking meaning either requesting or questioning.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه خطاب لنبينا صلى الله عليه وسلم والسؤال بمعناه المشهور إلا أن الجمهور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: His reported past-tense reading فسأل without hamza, also attributed to the Prophet's recitation, identifies Moses as the questioner and makes the command consequent on God's giving him the signs.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس فسأل على صيغة الماضي بغير همز كقال وهي لغة قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Moses is addressed, he may be told to ask Pharaoh to release Israel, ask the Israelites for support, or ask whether they remained faithful or followed Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: أي فقلنا له اطلبهم من فرعون وقل له أرسل معي بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: If Muhammad is addressed, he asks learned People of Scripture to confirm the event as established in their books, as provocation or emphasis rather than for information.
rows.anchor: والمعنى فاسأل يا محمد مؤمني أهل الكتاب عن ذلك إما لأن تظاهر الأدلة أقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the Muhammad-address reading, إذ جاءهم can attach to an implied ذكر or to an implied response telling the event; attaching it to سل fails because his question was not contemporaneous with Moses' arrival.
rows.anchor: ولا يصح تعلقه بسل إذ ليس سؤاله صلى الله عليه وسلم في وقت مجيء موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively فاسأل may be an interpolated prompt like زيد فأعلم; then إذ جاءهم attaches to آتينا, avoiding an implied clause.
rows.anchor: نعم جعل الذاهبون إلى الأول فاسأل اعتراضا من باب زيد فأعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Further parses attach إذ جاءهم to an implied telling or remembering, or treat it as causal; objections include that أخبر takes ب or عن and that the telling did not occur when Moses arrived.
rows.anchor: اعترض أيضا بأن السؤال عن الآيات والجواب بالإخبار عن وقت المجيء أو ذكره لا يلائمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On a Muhammad-address reading, جاءهم can refer to the forefathers of the Israelites then present, requiring an omitted possessive or a kind of semantic shift; analogous options hold for any listener addressed.
rows.anchor: على سائر احتمالات كون الخطاب لنبينا عليه الصلاة والسلام إذجاء آباءهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The فـ in فقال is explanatory, implying that Moses went to Pharaoh, claimed prophethood, and showed a miracle before Pharaoh spoke.
rows.anchor: والفاء في ( فقال ) على سائر الاحتمالات والأوجه فصيحة

rows.speaker: فرعون
rows.claim: Pharaoh calls Moses مسحورا, meaning bewitched and mentally disordered, which supposedly explains his speech and claims.
rows.anchor: سحرت فاختل عقلك ولذلك اختل كلامك وادعيت ما ادعيت

rows.speaker: الفراء والطبري
rows.claim: They interpret مسحورا as ساحرا, by relational usage or literally, fitting the miracle interpretation of the signs.
rows.anchor: مسحورا بمعنى ساحرا على النسب أو حقيقة وهو يناسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses answers Pharaoh: his knowledge that these signs came only from the Creator and governor of heaven and earth proves Moses is neither bewitched nor a sorcerer, and that his speech is sound; Pharaoh's royal ambition drives his denial.
rows.anchor: وحاصل الرد أن علمك بأن هاتيك الآيات من الله تعالى إذ لا يقدر عليها سواه تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: He notes that Moses' attribution to the Lord of heaven and earth recalls Pharaoh's opening question about the Lord of the worlds, exposing Pharaoh's lack of control and impossible claim to divinity; Pharaoh knows the signs' origin but obstinately denies it.
rows.anchor: لما سأله فرعون في أول محاورته فقال له : وما رب العالمين قال : رب السموات والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses addresses Pharaoh as rebuke: the point is not to inform him of his own knowledge, but to confront him as one who knows the obvious signs.
rows.anchor: وخاطبه بذلك على سبيل التوبيخ أي أنت بحال من يعلم هذه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another cited verse says Pharaoh and his followers denied the signs despite inward certainty and wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: وجحدوا بها واستيقنتها أنفسهم ظلما وعلوا

rows.speaker: علي وزيد بن علي والكسائي
rows.claim: They read علمت with a first-person subject: Moses says that he knows the signs were sent only by the Creator and governor of the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: بضم التاء فيكون موسى عليه السلام قد أخبر عن نفسه

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report attributes to Ali the statement that Pharaoh did not know; Moses was the one who knew. Abu Hayyan rejects the report because its transmitter Kulthum al-Muradi is unknown and the attribution seems implausible.
rows.anchor: والله ما علم عدو الله تعالى ولكن موسى عليه السلام هو الذي علم

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti cites transmitters who report Ali reciting the verb with ḍamma and saying this; Abu Hayyan's unidentified transmitter may occur in their chains.
rows.anchor: أن سعيد بن منصور وابن المنذر وابن أبي حاتم أخرجوا عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه أنه كان يقرأ بالضم

rows.speaker: الحوفي وأبو البقاء وابن عطية
rows.claim: They parse بصائر as a circumstantial accusative attached to أنزل; the author notes disagreement over whether a dependent word can follow an excepted phrase and says many grammarians instead posit an implied verb.
rows.anchor: حال من هؤلاء والعامل فيه أنزل المذكور عند الحوفي وأبي البقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: بصائر means manifest signs that let observers see Moses' truth, rational proofs, or lessons; it derives as a plural of بصيرة meaning an illuminating proof.
rows.anchor: أي بينات مكشوفات تبصرك صدقي على أنه جمع بصيرة بمعنى مبصرة أي بينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the nine are the reported commandments, هؤلاء could point to Moses' displayed miracles; taking it to mean the laws themselves assumes they were all established by the dialogue and requires some interpretive strain.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن تكون ( هؤلاء ) إشارة إلى ما أظهره عليه السلام من المعجزات

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
rows.claim: They explain مثبورا as destroyed, the author's clearest interpretation.
rows.anchor: هالكا كما روي عن الحسن ومجاهد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He explains مثبورا as turned away from good and stamped with evil, from the idiom asking what blocked someone.
rows.anchor: أي مصروفا عن الخير مطبوعا على الشر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report via al-Tusti glosses the word as accursed or held back from good; other reports give deficient in reason, bewitched, or مخالف, with Anas objecting that prophets do not curse or insult.
rows.anchor: من تفسيره بملعونا محبوسا عن الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers destroyed as the strongest gloss and says the harsh tone does not conflict with the earlier order to speak gently: after God reassured Moses, he could address Pharaoh forcefully; Moses' true expectation and Pharaoh's false suspicion differ greatly.
rows.anchor: إننا نخاف أن يفرط علينا أو أن يطغى

rows.speaker: أبي وابن كعب
rows.claim: They read وإن أخالك يا فرعون مثبورا with a lightened إن and a distinguishing lām; أخال means I think, normally with kasra though fatḥa also occurs.
rows.anchor: وإن أخالك يا فرعون مثبورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: استفزاز is originally disturbance and here euphemizes Pharaoh's expulsion of Moses and his people from Egypt or from all the earth; expulsion implies killing and extermination.
rows.anchor: وأصل الاستفزاز الإزعاج وكنى به عن إخراجهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God reverses Pharaoh's plan: the drowning expels Pharaoh and his followers instead, an especially clear reversal if Pharaoh meant the whole earth and still a reversal if he meant Egypt.
rows.anchor: أي فعكسنا عليه مكره حيث أراد ذلك لهم دونه فكان له دونهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's instruction came through Moses after Pharaoh's drowning, or after the drowning of Pharaoh and his followers; it addresses the Israelites Pharaoh sought to expel.
rows.anchor: على لسان موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The land may be Egypt if Israelites returned after the exodus and pursuit, or refer to descendants of the targeted Israelites if that return is unconfirmed; others identify it as the Holy Land, Syria.
rows.anchor: وهذا ظاهر أن ثبت أنهم دخلوها بعد أن خرجوا منها وأتبعهم فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final promise may mean the final return, afterlife, Hour, or final abode; each reading points to the resurrection.
rows.anchor: أي الكرة أو الحياة أو الساعة أو الدار الآخرة والمراد على جميع ذلك قيام الساعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He glosses لفيفا as all together; the author explains it as a mixed multitude later divided into the saved and the wretched.
rows.anchor: أي مختلطين أنتم وهم ثم نحكم بينكم ونميز سعداءكم من أشقيائكم وأصل اللفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لفيف can be a collective noun for a crowd from varied tribes without a singular, or a verbal noun covering few and many; grammarians also say بكم makes the addressed group stand for both them and you.
rows.anchor: تغليب المخاطبين على الغائبين والمراد بهم وبكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage returns to the Qur'an and links back to the challenge in 17:88; Arab discourse may digress through several topics and then return, as conversation branches.
rows.anchor: عود إلى شرح حال القرآن الكريم فهو مرتبط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to the Qur'an; readings referring it to Moses, the nine signs, or the earlier promise are remote because the verse is tied to its surrounding discussion.
rows.anchor: فضمير الغائب للقرآن وأبعد من ذهب إلى أنه لموسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the preferred reading both occurrences of bi are circumstantial: revelation came with the divine wisdom requiring it, and its descent came with the truth it contains; alternatives make the first causal and second circumstantial, or both causal.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الباء في الموضعين للملابسة والجار والمجرور في موضع الحال من ضمير القرآن

rows.speaker: أبو سليمان الدمشقي
rows.claim: He takes the first truth as monotheism and the second as promise, threat, command, and prohibition.
rows.anchor: الحق الأول التوحيد والثاني الوعد والوعيد والأمر والنهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the truth is God's preserved decree: angels guard the Qur'an from satanic interference both during revelation and descent; another identifies the second truth with the Prophet, a remote reading.
rows.anchor: وقيل الحق في الموضعين الأمر المحفوظ الثابت والمعنى

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: He regards the second clause as a meaning-level reinforcement of the first; others avoid calling it repetition because sending down and descending differ, and say the second clause rules out an obstruction to descent.
rows.anchor: ونحى الطبري إلى أن الجملة الثانية توكيد للأولى من حيث المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was sent only to announce reward to the obedient and warn sinners, not to force challenging disbelievers into faith or guarantee their guidance.
rows.anchor: فلا عليك إلا التبشير والإنذار لا هداية الكفرة المقترحين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قرآنا is accusative through an implied verb explained by فرقناه, an اشتغال construction; a nominative start is also possible if its indefiniteness has a licensing context.
rows.anchor: نصب بفعل مضمر يفسره قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He attaches the accusative to أرسلناك, as in saying that the Prophet was sent as a mercy and a Qur'an; the author calls this strained.
rows.anchor: هو منصوب بأرسلناك

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He also permits coordination with the كاف in أرسلناك, which the author treats as an astonishing parse.
rows.anchor: ومما يقضي منه العجب ما جوزه ابن عطية من نصبه بالعطف على الكاف

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: He proposes an implied verb indicated by آتينا or أرسلناك, a parse ranked below the initial explanation but above the remaining alternatives.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء : وهو دون الأول وفوق ما عداه إنه منصوب بفعل مضمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فرقناه means either that God sent it down in successive portions or that the Qur'an distinguishes truth from falsehood, the latter involving an omitted preposition; Ibn Abbas also glosses it as explaining lawful and unlawful rulings.
rows.anchor: أي أنزلناه منجما مفرقا أو فرقنا فيه بين الحق والباطل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He glosses فرقناه as perfected and separated, as in the verse about every wise matter being distinguished.
rows.anchor: أحكمناه وفصلناه كما في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وأبي وعبد الله
rows.claim: They and other named readers pronounce فرقناه with a doubled rā; it still means gradual revelation, with the doubled form intensifying repeated separation. The author prefers this explanation over the proposed contrast between near and far separation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه وابن عباس وأبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations divide the Qur'an into commands, rulings, admonitions, examples, stories, reports, and prophecies; most commentators take gradual revelation.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه فرقنا آياته بين أمر ونهي وحكم وأحكام ومواعظ وأمثال وقصص

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says the whole Qur'an moved from the Preserved Tablet to the angelic scribes in the lower heaven, then Gabriel delivered it to the Prophet in portions over twenty years; variants give twenty, twenty-three, or twenty-five years after placement in Bayt al-Izza, with al-Bahr attributing the variance to disagreement about the Prophet's age.
rows.anchor: نزل القرآن جملة واحدة من عند الله تعالى من اللوح المحفوظ إلى السفرة الكرام الكاتبين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: A report through Qatada says revelation took eighteen years, eight in Mecca and ten after migration; Ibn Atiyya calls this confused and unauthentic, while the relied-on span is twenty-three years.
rows.anchor: من طريق قتادة عن الحسن كان يقول

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: A report in al-Bayhaqi says Gabriel delivered the Qur'an five verses at a time, so Umar advised learning five verses at a time.
rows.anchor: تعلموا القرآن خمس آيات خمس آيات فإن جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: He taught five verses in the morning and five in the evening, saying Gabriel brought the Qur'an in groups of five; the author qualifies this as the usual pattern, since sound reports attest both larger and smaller portions.
rows.anchor: كان أبو سعيد الخدري يعلمنا القرآن خمس ءايات بالغداة

rows.speaker: أبي وعبد الله
rows.claim: They add عليك after فرقناه, making the reading say that God apportioned the Qur'an to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: فرقناه عليك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: على مكث means with deliberation and measured pace, making memorization easier and understanding better; another view means over a long period, gradually.
rows.anchor: أي تؤدة وتأن فإنه أيسر للحفظ وأعون على الفهم روي ذلك عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians differ whether على مكث attaches to فرقناه or لتقرأه; it may be object plus circumstantial phrase, a circumstantial accusative, or an implied noun. Abu al-Baqa takes it as a state; al-Hawfi's proposed apposition to على الناس is rejected because مكث describes reader or recitation, not people.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر لا يبالي بتعلق هذين الحرفين بما ذكر الاختلاف معناهما لأن الأول في موضع المفعول به

rows.speaker: القراء وابن عطية
rows.claim: مكث is read with ḍamma or fatḥa, not kasra; Ibn Atiyya claims consensus on ḍamma.
rows.anchor: والمكث مثلث الميم وقريء بالضم والفتح ولم يقرأ بالكسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an was sent down in stages according to events and benefits; this restates the gradual division while explaining its purpose.
rows.anchor: على حسب الحوادث والمصالح فذكر هذا بعد قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to believe or disbelieve means the Qur'an's perfection does not depend on their belief and is not diminished by their denial.
rows.anchor: على معنى أن إيمانكم به وعدم إيمانكم به سواء لأن إيمانكم لا يزيده كمالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those given knowledge before the Qur'an are scriptural scholars who recognized revelation and prophetic signs, or people who saw the Prophet's and revelation's descriptions in earlier books.
rows.anchor: أي العلماء الذين قرءوا الكتب السالفة من قبل تنزل القرآن وعرفوا حقيقة الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: خرورا is falling quickly; أذقان means chins, by extension the face, and Ibn Abbas is reported to take it as faces; their literal prostration is worship or gratitude for the promised prophethood.
rows.anchor: الخرور السقوط بسرعة والأذقان جمع ذقن وهو مجتمع اللحيين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: A figurative reading takes falling on chins as complete obedience and humility; he says the chin is named because it is the first part of a prostrating face to reach the ground.
rows.anchor: فأخرج الكلام على سبيل الاستعارة التمثيلية وفسر الخرور للأذقان بالسقوط على الوجوه الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers literal prostration; he raises the objection that forehead and nose land first, then explains that the chin is the nearest part when a fall begins. Other proposals involve actual chin-first collapse or an unfamiliar form of prostration.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن هنا خرورا وسجودا على الحقيقة وقيل : لاشيء

rows.speaker: صاحب الفرائد
rows.claim: He explains the chin as hyperbole for pressing the forehead and nose so firmly that the chin seems glued to the earth; the author calls this a very good interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب الفرائد المراد المبالغة في التحامل على الجبهة والأنف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He takes the lām as expressing اختصاص: they assign their chins specifically to falling in prostration.
rows.anchor: واللام على ما نص عليه الزمخشري للاختصاص وذكر أن المعنى جعلوا أذقانهم للخرور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām need not mean exclusive chin-only contact: it can mark a particular relation or direction, so the phrase depicts falling to earth; some instead take it as على.
rows.anchor: وتعقبه الخفاجي بأنه مبني على أن الاختصاص الذي تدل عليه اللام بمعنى الحصر وليس كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The view that به and قبله refer to the Prophet is contradicted by context; reports from Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Jarir that يتلى refers to the earlier scripture are also weak.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعض عود ضميري ( به وقبله ) عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: The clause may be inside the command as its rationale: even if you do not believe, the learned believe sincerely; alternatively it consoles the Prophet outside the command. Al-Kashf sees consolation as central, with reproach secondary or vice versa.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الجملة الإسمية داخلة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He reads believe or disbelieve as a threat to unbelievers, contrasted with earlier People of the Book who humbled themselves when scripture was recited; the author finds this distant and strained.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية يتوجه في الآية معنى آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They glorify their Lord as free from failing his promise, or from the deniers' disbelief and false claims.
rows.anchor: في سجودهم أو مطلقا ( سبحان ربنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: إن is lightened from its doubled form, with an implicit pronoun of شأن and the lām as a separator: the matter is certainly so.
rows.anchor: إن مخففة من المثقلة واسمها ضمير شأن واللام فارقة أي إن الشأن هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their second fall differs in cause from the first: the first expresses awe or gratitude for the promise, the second responds to the Qur'an's admonitions.
rows.anchor: كرر الخرور للأذقان لاختلاف السبب فإن الأول لتعظيم أمر الله تعالى أو الشكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They weep from fear of God; the verbal clause conveys recurring renewal because reflection continually renews that fear.
rows.anchor: أي باكين من خشية الله تعالى ولما كان البكاء ناشئا من الخشية الناشئة من التفكر

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from al-Nadr ibn Sa'd promises that a servant's weeping can save a community from fire, that tears quench fire, and that fear-driven tears protect the eye and face; the author states no grading.
rows.anchor: عن النضر بن سعد قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لو أن عبدا بكى

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports the Prophet saying that two eyes are untouched by fire: one that weeps from fear of God and one that guards in God's path overnight.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال : سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that one who weeps from fear will not enter Hell until milk returns to the udder; dust from God's path and Hell's smoke will never meet on a servant.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: عبد الأعلى التيمي
rows.claim: He says knowledge that does not make its possessor weep is likely unbeneficial, since God describes the learned as weeping; the report is transmitted by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الأعلى التيمي أنه قال : إن من أوتي من العلم ما لا يبكيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an increases their reverence as they hear it by adding knowledge and certainty about God's command to what their evidence had already established.
rows.anchor: لأن الله تعالى نعت أهل العلم فقال ( ويخرون للأذقان يبكون ) ( ويزيدهم ( أي القرآن بسماعهم

none: The source text is broken; only the isolated letter م appears.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One occasion report says that in Mecca the Prophet invoked God as Allah and Rahman; polytheists accused him of worshipping two gods, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال : صلى صلى الله عليه وسلم بمكة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Another occasion report says People of the Book complained that the Prophet rarely mentioned Rahman although it appears often in the Torah, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: وعن الضحاك أنه قال : قال أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the polytheist occasion, the two names are equally names for one divine essence, so monotheism concerns the single worshipped entity; this coheres with the following denial of a child or partner.
rows.anchor: والمراد على الأول التسوية بين اللفظين بأنهما عبارتان عن ذات واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the Jewish occasion, the names are equally apt for invocation; their preference for Rahman may reflect its frequent Torah mention. A proposed wisdom is that Moses' anger made abundant mention of mercy beneficial for his community.
rows.anchor: وعلى الثاني التسوية في حسن الإطلاق والإفضاء إلى المقصود

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: He finds the Jewish occasion more fitting because describing the names as beautiful presupposes that listeners thought one name better than another.
rows.anchor: وهذا أوجب لقوله تبارك اسمه

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: He says the answer in both contexts is equality among the two names: one good name suffices against the Torah preference, and the names point to one perfect divine being rather than two gods.
rows.anchor: الغرض على الوجهين التسوية بين اللفظين في الحسن

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: He distinguishes the complaints: Jews objected to preferring one name, while polytheists objected to combining them; أيا ما تدعوا fits the Jews if أو means choice and the polytheists if it permits both names.
rows.anchor: ووجه الطيبي الأجوبية بأن اعتراض اليهود كان تعبيرا للمسلمين على ترجيح

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: He says the ideal direct answer to the Jews would have been that Allah is preferred because it gathers every perfection, unlike Rahman; if أو means permission, the verse instead directly permits the polytheists to combine names.
rows.anchor: إنما رجحنا الله على الرحمن في الذكر لأنه جامع لجميع صفات الكمال

rows.speaker: الجلبي
rows.claim: He argues that the fronted predicate فله الأسماء الحسنى means all names belong to God alone, answering the polytheist claim of multiple gods; since using both names is possible, he takes أو as permission rather than exclusive choice.
rows.anchor: ومنع الأجوبية أيضا الجلبي بأن تقديم الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says any restriction focuses on the names' beauty rather than ownership, choice remains possible, and reason permits combining nonconflicting names; he sides with denying that the clause is the conditional answer and with reading أو as permission.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الحق مع مانع الأجوبية والقائل بالإباحة

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: He reads الدعاء as calling or invoking; al-Zamakhshari instead reads it as naming, with an omitted object and perhaps an omitted ب. The author reports objections about duplicate meanings or coordinating one divine referent with itself, and counters that the wording may name the names and that their distinct concepts suffice.
rows.anchor: والدعاء على ما اختاره أبو حيان وجماعة بمعنى النداء

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: He sees al-Zamakhshari's naming interpretation as favoring the polytheist occasion; if the verse addresses polytheists it names God, while on a Jewish occasion it invokes God.
rows.anchor: وجعل الطيبي لذلك تفسير الزمخشري إياه بالتسمية مؤذنا بميله إلى أنه رد على المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أيا is a jussive conditional pronoun functioning as object, its tanwin replaces a genitive, and ما is emphatic or itself marks the condition; Talha ibn Musarrif reads من, parsed as extra or conditional, with two conditional particles together attested only exceptionally.
rows.anchor: اسم شرط جازم منصوب بتدعوا وجازم له فهو عامل ومعمول

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unattributed poetic line illustrates the rare combining of two prepositions that is compared to combining two conditional particles.
rows.anchor: فأصبحن لا يسألنني عن بما به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فله الأسماء الحسنى functions where the conditional answer belongs but gives its rationale instead, intensifying the point; the implied wording is that whichever name you invoke is good because God has the beautiful names.
rows.anchor: واقعة موقع جواب الشرط وهي في الحقيقة تعليل له

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: On the permission reading, calling God by either name is sound and using both is even better, as God commands invocation by the beautiful names; he reconstructs a concise or expanded conditional answer, which the author leaves as a strained account.
rows.anchor: فبأيهما سميته فأنت مصيب وإن سميته بهما جميعا فأنت أصوب

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: A proposal to pause at أيا and treat ما تدعوا as an independent conditional clause is rejected: ما does not refer to rational individuals, and the condition would wrongly claim universal scope.
rows.anchor: على معنى أي اللفظين تدعوه به جاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in فله refers to the named or invoked entity understood from context, because names belong to their bearer rather than to a name or spoken title.
rows.anchor: عائد على المسمى أو المنادى المفهوم من الكلام والقرينة عقلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The beautiful names denote the divine essence gathering all attributes of perfection, majesty, beauty, and generosity.
rows.anchor: ووصف الأسماء بالحسنى لدلالتها على ما هو جامع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews apparently accepted the beauty of God's other names but believed Rahman the most beloved, greatest, and noblest because it occurs frequently in the Torah; Muslims too recognize differences in rank among names.
rows.anchor: إن الظاهر مما روي عن اليهود أنهم لا ينكرون حسن سائر أسمائه تعالى

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet heard a man invoke God as the One, the Eternal Refuge who neither begets nor is begotten and has no equal, and swore that he had invoked by God's greatest name, which guarantees response.
rows.anchor: اللهم إني أسألك بأني أشهد أن لا إله إلا أنت الأحد الصمد

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Another report locates the greatest name in the verse naming God as one, without deity but Him, the Merciful, and in the opening of Al Imran naming the Living and Sustaining.
rows.anchor: اسم الله تعالى الأعظم في هاتين الآيتين

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali says Allah is the greatest of the ninety-nine names because it denotes the essence containing all divine attributes and is uniquely exclusive to God; other names typically denote single qualities and can be applied to others.
rows.anchor: على أن الله أعظم الأسماء التسعة والتسعين لأنه دال على الذات الجامعة لصفات الإلهية كلها

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: He says Rahman is also exclusive to God and therefore close to Allah, though derived from mercy, explaining why the two are paired here; the honor of selected ninety-nine names reflects the dignity of their meanings.
rows.anchor: واسمه تعالى الرحمن لا يسمى به غيره تعالى أيضا وهو من هذا الوجه قريب من اسم الله

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says singling out Allah and Rahman implies they surpass other names, and putting Allah first signals its greater rank; this reading most directly answers the Jewish claim of a preferred name, though reports also rank names and may favor the polytheist occasion.
rows.anchor: تخصيص هذين الإسمين يعني الله والرحمن بالذكر يدل على أنهما أشرف من سائر الأسماء

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: He argues that if God created injustice, an unjust act could yield a divine name, contradicting the claim that all divine names are beautiful; the author denies the entailment because creating something does not make it God's attribute or a proper name.
rows.anchor: واحتج الجبائي بالآية على أنه تعالى ليس خالق الظلم وإلا لصح اشتقاق اسم له سبحانه منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although God creates all things, reverence counsels against calling Him creator of the ugly; His name is Creator without qualification, or Creator of everything.
rows.anchor: نعم لا ينبغي أن يقال لله تبارك وتعالى خالق القبيح للزوم الأدب معه سبحانه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A route through Nahshal ibn Sa'id and al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas is cited for calling this a protection verse, but the transmitted report is cut off before its content appears.
rows.anchor: من طريق نهشل بن سعيد عن الضحاك عن ابن عباس أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
